questions.prompt: There are four towns P, Q, R and T. Q is to the South-West of P, R is to the East of Q and South-East of P and T is to the North of R in line with Q, P. In which direction of P is T located?
hints: Draw Q below and left of P, and place R directly east of Q.
The line through Q and P has positive slope. Its intersection with the northward line from R lies beyond P.
questions.solution: Take P=(0,0), Q=(-a,-b), with a,b>0. Since R is east of Q and southeast of P, R=(c,-b), c>0. The QP line is y=(b/a)x. T is directly north of R on this line, so T=(c,bc/a). Both coordinates are positive, hence T is northeast of P.
questions.theory: Compass directions can be modeled using Cartesian coordinates: east is positive x and north is positive y. A point northeast of another has both coordinate differences positive; southeast has positive x and negative y. Collinearity means the three positions lie on one straight line, expressible by a linear equation. The phrase directly north imposes equal x coordinates, whereas east imposes equal y coordinates. A useful method is to assign symbolic positive distances rather than invent equal distances that the question does not supply. Determine signs before numerical magnitudes. A common pitfall is assuming that northeast necessarily makes a forty-five-degree angle, or treating a general compass direction as an exact distance.

similar_questions.prompt: P=(0,0), Q=(-2,-3), and R=(4,-3). Find the point north of R on line QP.
similar_questions.solution: Line QP is y=3x/2. At x=4 it gives y=6. Thus T=(4,6), northeast of P.

similar_questions.prompt: P=(0,0), Q=(3,-2), R=(-3,-2). Find the point north of R on QP.
similar_questions.solution: The line is y=-2x/3. At x=-3, y=2, so T=(-3,2), northwest of P.

questions.prompt: A certain sum of money becomes double of itself in 5 years at simple rate of interest. In how many years will it become 16 times of itself at the same rate of simple interest?
hints: Simple interest grows by a fixed fraction of the principal each year.
Doubling means interest equals one principal; sixteenfold means interest equals fifteen principals.
questions.solution: For principal P and annual rate r, A=P(1+rt). At t=5, 2P=P(1+5r), giving r=1/5. For A=16P, 16=1+t/5, hence t=75 years.
questions.theory: Simple interest is calculated on the original principal throughout the investment, not on previously earned interest. With principal P, annual fractional rate r and time t in years, interest is Prt and total amount is P(1+rt). Thus the amount is an affine, rather than exponential, function of time. If the amount reaches m times the principal in time T, then r=(m-1)/T. Another target multiple n takes T(n-1)/(m-1) years. All times must use the same units as the quoted rate. The crucial distinction is between interest and total amount: a sixteenfold amount contains only fifteen principals of interest. Applying repeated doubling instead would incorrectly assume compound interest.

similar_questions.prompt: A principal triples in 8 years at simple interest. When does it become sevenfold?
similar_questions.solution: 8r=2 gives r=1/4. Sevenfold requires rt=6, so t=24 years.

questions.prompt: In which of the following, entropy will decrease?
hints: Identify the system whose thermodynamic entropy is being compared.
Heating, protein unfolding and aggregation compete during cooking; a visibly rigid egg does not establish an entropy decrease.
questions.solution: The source does not specify a system, initial/final temperatures or conditions. Heating water and melting ice normally increase the material entropy; dissolution is ordinarily associated with increased mixing entropy, though a complete thermodynamic statement needs conditions. The fourth choice is often intended as a qualitative claim that coagulation makes an egg more ordered. That is not a sufficient thermodynamic derivation: boiling includes heating, unfolding proteins and aggregation, and the net egg entropy cannot be determined from the words alone. For an isolated egg-water-environment system the total entropy cannot decrease. Therefore no option is rigorously implied by the literal source, and no answer is assigned. Conditional intended reading: if “entropy” is only a simplified measure of structural ordering during coagulation and heating/unfolding are deliberately ignored, the intended choice is D; that extra convention is absent.
questions.theory: Thermodynamic entropy S is a state function defined for a reversible heat transfer by dS=δQ_rev/T. The second law requires the entropy of an isolated system to be nondecreasing; a subsystem may lose entropy by exporting heat or matter. Entropy changes must therefore specify system boundaries and states. For a phase transition at equilibrium, ΔS=L/T, with positive latent heat for melting or vaporization. Heating a material with positive heat capacity produces ΔS=∫C(T)dT/T>0. Molecular ordering alone is not a reliable substitute for thermodynamic accounting, especially when denaturation, aggregation and heating occur together. The method is to identify states, include all energy and matter exchanges, and separate subsystem entropy from total entropy.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the entropy change when 100 J of heat reversibly melts ice at 273 K.
similar_questions.solution: At constant transition temperature ΔS=Q_rev/T=100/273≈0.366 J/K, positive.

similar_questions.prompt: A body loses 60 J reversibly at 300 K to a reservoir at the same temperature. Find both entropy changes.
similar_questions.solution: The body changes by -60/300=-0.2 J/K. The reservoir gains +0.2 J/K, so the combined reversible entropy change is zero.

questions.prompt: There are two numbers such that the difference between them is 10 and their ratio is 5:3. Find the product of these two numbers.
hints: Represent the numbers using a common multiplier.
Their difference is two times that multiplier.
questions.solution: Write the numbers as 5k and 3k. Their positive difference is 2k=10, so k=5. They are 25 and 15, whose product is 375.
questions.theory: A ratio a:b states that two quantities share the form ak and bk for one common scale factor k. It determines relative size but not absolute size; an additional sum, difference or product fixes k. For a positive difference d and a>b, k=d/(a-b) and the product is ab d²/(a-b)². These formulas require the quantities to be measured in compatible units. If “difference” means absolute difference, a negative common factor may also satisfy the numerical relationship, but the product remains unchanged. The reliable method is to introduce the common multiplier, translate the remaining condition into an equation, and then recover the requested quantity. Do not replace a ratio by an additive difference.

questions.prompt: Suppose there are 9 identical gold-coins out of which 8 coins have same weight. One coin is counterfeit and weighs slightly less than the other coins. You have a classical balance scale for weighing. What is the minimum number of weighings required to definitively isolate and identify the counterfeit coin?
hints: Each balance weighing has three possible outcomes.
Divide nine coins into three equal groups; first identify the suspect group, then its suspect coin.
questions.solution: One weighing gives only three outcomes and cannot distinguish nine possibilities, so at least two are needed. Weigh coins 1–3 against 4–6. If equal, the lighter coin is among 7–9; otherwise it belongs to the lighter pan. In the suspect triple weigh one coin against another. A lighter pan identifies the counterfeit; equality identifies the third coin. Thus two weighings suffice and are minimal.
questions.theory: A balance scale yields three distinguishable outcomes: left lighter, right lighter, or equality. A decision procedure using k weighings can have at most 3^k terminal outcome sequences, so identifying one known-light counterfeit among N candidates requires 3^k≥N. This is an information lower bound; to prove minimality one must also give a strategy attaining it. When the counterfeit is known lighter, partitioning candidates into three equal groups and comparing two groups gives a ternary search. Equality selects the unweighed group, while imbalance selects the lighter group. If the counterfeit could instead be heavier or lighter, the state space and valid strategies change. The common pitfall is applying a two-outcome binary search model to a three-outcome balance.

similar_questions.prompt: Identify a known-light counterfeit among 27 coins. What is the minimum?
similar_questions.solution: At least log_3 27=3 weighings are necessary. Compare two groups of nine, then two groups of three in the suspect nine, then two individual coins in the suspect triple. Exactly three suffice.

similar_questions.prompt: Identify a known-light counterfeit among 3 coins.
similar_questions.solution: Compare coin 1 with coin 2. The lighter coin is false; equality makes coin 3 false. One weighing is necessary and sufficient.

questions.prompt: The largest possible triangle is inscribed in a semi-circle of diameter 14 cm. What would be the area inside the semi-circle which is not occupied by the triangle?
hints: Use the diameter as base and maximize the perpendicular height.
The radius is 7 cm, so the maximal triangle has area (14)(7)/2.
questions.solution: The maximal triangle has the diameter as base and the top of the semicircle as third vertex, giving area 49 cm². To justify maximality, slide a lowest vertex down to the diameter without decreasing area, and extend its diameter-side base to both endpoints; the resulting area is at most 14×7/2. The semicircle area is 49π/2. The remainder is 49π/2−49≈27.969 cm², which is 28 cm² to the precision of the choices (exactly 28 with π≈22/7).
questions.theory: The area of a triangle is half the product of its base and the perpendicular height. A circle of radius r has area πr², and a semicircle has area πr²/2. In a semicircle, the largest triangle uses the full diameter as base and the maximum available height r; its area is r². One can justify this by lowering the lowest vertex to the diameter, then moving diameter-side vertices to the endpoints, operations that do not reduce the available area. The uncovered area is consequently r²(π/2−1). Keep the exact π expression until numerical evaluation. A common pitfall is using the full circle area or calling the diameter the triangle height. Integer options may encode conventional rounding.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the maximum triangle area in a semicircle of radius 5.
similar_questions.solution: Base is 10 and maximal height is 5, so area=10×5/2=25 square units.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the uncovered area for that maximal triangle when r=2.
similar_questions.solution: Semicircle area=2π and triangle area=4. The remainder is 2π−4≈2.283 square units.

questions.prompt: During the interaction of population of two different species identify the type where only one species is benefited and is detrimental to the other species.
hints: Encode the effects on each species as positive, negative or neutral.
You need a positive-negative interaction in both listed examples.
questions.solution: Parasitism benefits the parasite and harms the host; predation benefits the predator and harms the prey. Both have the (+,−) interaction pattern. Commensalism is (+,0), amensalism is (−,0), and competition is (−,−), so the other pairs do not meet the stated condition.
questions.theory: Ecological interactions classify the effect of one species on another, often using plus for benefit, minus for harm and zero for negligible effect. Mutualism has the pattern (+,+), commensalism (+,0), amensalism (−,0), competition (−,−), and predation or parasitism (+,−). These signs describe effects relative to a suitable baseline, usually survival, growth or reproduction. Predators consume prey; parasites derive resources from a host while typically maintaining a longer association. The classification is qualitative and can depend on environmental context. For a paired-choice question, both members of the option must have the required sign pattern. A frequent error is choosing any harmful interaction without checking whether the other participant actually benefits.

similar_questions.prompt: A tapeworm obtains nutrients from a mammal and weakens it. Classify the interaction.
similar_questions.solution: The worm benefits (+), and the host is harmed (−). This is parasitism, a (+,−) interaction.

similar_questions.prompt: A bird nests in a tree without materially affecting the tree. Classify the interaction.
similar_questions.solution: The bird benefits (+), the tree is approximately unaffected (0), so this is commensalism rather than parasitism.

questions.theory: Letter-series questions can be analyzed by assigning letters their ordered alphabet positions. For grouped terms, examine each position across terms separately, then verify that the same proposed rule reproduces every given term. questions.prompt: The pie chart shows employees by department: Accounts 12%, Admin 20%, Teaching 40%, Non teaching 28%. Male:Female ratios are Accounts 7:5, Admin 2:3, Teaching 5:3, Non teaching 3:4. Total employees = 2000. What is the ratio between female employees in Admin and non teaching departments?
hints: Convert each department percentage to its total employee count.
Female fractions are 3/5 in Admin and 4/7 in non teaching.
questions.solution: Admin has 0.20×2000=400 employees, of whom 400×3/5=240 are female. Non teaching has 0.28×2000=560 employees, of whom 560×4/7=320 are female. Their ratio is 240:320=3:4.
questions.theory: A pie-chart percentage describes a fraction of the entire population, while an internal male:female ratio describes a split within one category. If the population is N, a category share is p and its male:female ratio is a:b, then the female count is Np b/(a+b). The denominator must contain both ratio parts. Ratios between category subgroups can be computed without knowing N because the common population cancels, but actual counts provide a useful consistency check. The method is to multiply the overall fraction by the conditional fraction, then simplify the resulting ratio. Avoid interpreting a female ratio part as a percentage or comparing department totals when the question asks specifically about female employees.

questions.prompt: The present population of a city is 6000. If the number of males increases by 14% and the number of females increases by 22%, then the population will become 6900. What is the present population of females in the city?
hints: Let the present female population be F and male population be 6000−F.
The extra growth above 14% of everyone is 8% of F.
questions.solution: The new total is 1.14(6000−F)+1.22F=6840+0.08F. Equating to 6900 gives 0.08F=60 and F=750. The male count is 5250; checking, 5985+915=6900.
questions.theory: When two subpopulations have different growth rates, their combined growth rate is a weighted average using original population shares. If initial counts M and F have fractional increases a and b, the new total is (1+a)M+(1+b)F. With M+F=N, this becomes (1+a)N+(b−a)F, giving a single linear equation for F when the new total is known. This requires that the stated growth accounts for the complete change and that the categories partition the population. A useful check is that the observed overall growth lies between a and b. Do not average the two rates equally unless the two original populations have equal sizes; percentage changes use their respective original denominators.

questions.solution: Under the stem’s stated model, nonworking people do not directly contribute through the listed productive work, so their direct contribution is zero. The three listed working sectors contribute 38%, 28%, and 10%, all positive. Therefore nonworking population has the lowest direct contribution (D). If comparison were restricted to the sectors in the chart, agriculture would instead be the smallest sector. The answer uses the explicit working-contributor convention, not a claim that nonworking persons have no wider economic effects.
questions.theory: A percentage-share chart partitions a total into category contributions. If GDP is G and a sector share is p percent, its attributed output is Gp/100. Here the four plotted percentages add to one hundred, so the chart exhausts the stated output. Population share and output share have different denominators and cannot be directly compared; worker productivity would require sector-specific worker counts. The word contribution also needs a convention: this aptitude stem treats productive working people as the direct contributors, while nonworking population is outside that direct production model. The method is to identify the comparison set before finding a minimum. A frequent pitfall is automatically selecting the smallest plotted bar when an option describes a category outside the chart.

questions.prompt: Candidates in a competitive examination consisted of 60% men and 40% women. 70% of men and 75% of women cleared the qualifying test and entered the final test, where 80% men and 70% women were successful. Which statement is correct?

options.B: Success rate is higher for women
options.C: More men cleared the examination than women

hints: Multiply successive-stage fractions within each gender.
Use 1000 initial candidates to compare final counts and overall rates.
questions.solution: For 1000 initial candidates there are 600 men and 400 women. Qualifiers: 420 men and 300 women. Final successes: 420×0.8=336 men and 300×0.7=210 women. Overall success is 546/1000=54.6%, above 50%. Male success rate from the initial group is 56%, female rate is 52.5%. Thus only statement C is correct; more men also pass the qualifying stage.
questions.theory: Success in a sequence of tests requires passing every stage. Conditional probabilities therefore multiply: P(pass both|group)=P(pass first|group)P(pass final|passed first,group). Overall success is then a weighted sum across the initial group proportions, by the law of total probability. Counts and rates are distinct: a larger group can have more successful candidates even at a lower individual success rate. To analyze an aptitude question, choose a convenient hypothetical total such as 1000, compute stage counts and verify that every percentage uses the correct reference group. Do not add the two pass percentages or apply the final-stage percentage directly to all initial candidates without accounting for qualification.

questions.prompt: Two natural numbers have difference 6 and the difference between their squares is 60. Find the sum of their cubes.
hints: Factor the difference of squares.
The sum of the numbers is 60/6.
questions.solution: Let x>y. Then x−y=6 and x²−y²=(x−y)(x+y)=60, so x+y=10. Solving gives x=8 and y=2. The cube sum is 8³+2³=512+8=520.
questions.theory: The factorization x²−y²=(x−y)(x+y) converts a quadratic-looking condition into a product of the sum and difference. If a nonzero difference d and square difference K are known, the sum is K/d, and the numbers are ((K/d)+d)/2 and ((K/d)−d)/2. Natural-number requirements should be checked after solving: both expressions must be nonnegative or positive according to convention, and integral. Another useful identity is x³+y³=(x+y)³−3xy(x+y), with xy=((x+y)²−(x−y)²)/4. The method avoids unnecessary expansion or trial-and-error. A common pitfall is mistaking the difference of squares for the square of the difference; those differ by a cross term. Always verify the derived result by substituting it into the original hypotheses; this catches lost factors, extraneous roots and sign errors before comparing with the listed choices.

questions.prompt: Three alarm bells ring at intervals 30 sec, 40 sec and 45 sec respectively. They started simultaneously at 4:00 am. At what time will they all ring simultaneously?
hints: Seek the first positive time divisible by all three intervals.
Use prime factorizations to compute their least common multiple.
questions.solution: The next simultaneous ringing is after lcm(30,40,45) seconds. Factor 30=2×3×5, 40=2³×5 and 45=3²×5. The lcm is 2³×3²×5=360 seconds=6 minutes. Hence the next time is 4:06 am. The question’s usual convention asks for the next occurrence; later listed times may also be common occurrences (4:36 and 5:00), so “next” is implicit.
questions.theory: Events recurring every a,b,c units after a common start coincide exactly at nonnegative common multiples of those periods. The least positive coincidence is their least common multiple. For integers, prime factorization constructs the lcm by taking the largest exponent of each prime present in any period. In contrast, the greatest common divisor takes the smallest exponents and answers a different divisibility question. Time units must be standardized before calculation; convert seconds to minutes only after finding the common period. The method assumes exact periodic intervals and a synchronized starting instant. Aptitude formulations conventionally ask for the first later occurrence even when “next” is omitted. A pitfall is adding the periods or treating a common multiple as necessarily the least one.

questions.prompt: A process is used to separate substances in chemical mixtures. What is this process known as?
hints: Ask whether the stem specifies volatility, particle size, differential affinity or solubility.
Each listed process separates at least some chemical mixtures.
questions.solution: All four options are separation processes. Distillation separates components using volatility; filtration separates suspended solids using a porous barrier; chromatography separates components by differential distribution between mobile and stationary phases; crystallisation separates a solid through solubility and crystal formation. The stem supplies no mechanism, phases or mixture type that singles out one of these. Therefore a unique answer cannot be derived. Conditional intended reading: if the omitted defining feature were differential movement/affinity in mobile and stationary phases, C would follow; if it were different boiling points, A would follow. Neither condition is printed, so this item is a source issue.
questions.theory: Mixture separation exploits differences in physical or chemical properties rather than simply naming a universal operation. Distillation uses vapor–liquid equilibrium and differences in relative volatility, usually with heat and condensation. Filtration uses a permeable barrier to retain sufficiently large suspended particles while fluid passes. Chromatography uses differing interactions with a stationary phase and a moving carrier, producing differing migration or retention times. Crystallisation exploits solubility changes and crystal formation, often by cooling or evaporation. Selecting a technique requires information about the mixture, desired purity, component stability and contrasting properties. The method in a multiple-choice definition question is to match a specific mechanism, not merely a broad purpose shared by every answer. The missing mechanism here prevents unique selection.

similar_questions.prompt: Which method separates sand from water through filter paper?
similar_questions.solution: Sand is an insoluble suspended solid. The paper retains particles while water passes, so filtration is the specified process.

similar_questions.prompt: Which method separates ink pigments as a solvent moves along paper?

As with any finite pattern task, infinitely many contrived functions fit the samples; aptitude convention selects the simple common transformation. questions.prompt: Four positive integers A≤B≤C≤D have unique mode 6 and median 7. What is the minimum possible largest value D?

A unique mode 6 needs repetition, but three occurrences would force median 6.
questions.solution: The value 6 must occur at least twice; if three or four entries were 6, the median would be 6. Thus exactly two entries are 6. They cannot occupy the middle/right pair, because the median 7 requires B+C=14. Therefore A=B=6 and C=8. To keep 6 as the unique mode, D cannot equal 8; since D≥8 is integral, its least value is 9. The dataset 6,6,8,9 attains it.
questions.theory: For an ordered dataset with an even number of entries, the median is the average of its two central observations. A mode is a value with maximal frequency; a unique mode has strictly greater frequency than every other value. These are separate restrictions: the median controls central positions, while mode controls multiplicities. In a four-entry integer dataset, a unique mode normally requires one value to appear at least twice. Three occurrences force both central entries to equal that value. A useful method is to enumerate possible placements of the repeated mode under the order constraints, then impose the median equation and minimize the maximum. Do not accept a tied frequency as a unique mode; 6,6,8,8 has two modes.

similar_questions.prompt: Four positive integers have unique mode 4 and median 5. Minimize the largest.
similar_questions.solution: Exactly two entries are 4, so the ordered list begins 4,4. The median gives C=6. D must exceed 6 to avoid a second repeated value. Minimum D=7, attained by 4,4,6,7.

similar_questions.prompt: Find median and modes of 2,2,6,6.
similar_questions.solution: The median is (2+6)/2=4. Both 2 and 6 occur twice, so there are two modes and no unique mode.

questions.prompt: P+Q means P is the brother of Q; P×Q means P is the father of Q; P−Q means P is the sister of Q. Which relation shows that I is the niece of K?
hints: A niece is a female child of a sibling.
Find an option making K a sibling of I’s parent and I explicitly female.
questions.solution: B states K is brother of Y, Y is father of I, and I is sister of Z. Thus I is female and the daughter of K’s sibling Y, so I is K’s niece. A places I among K’s siblings, without specifying I’s sex. C makes I the father of Y and hence male. D makes K the father of Y and I a sister of Y, placing I as K’s child under the usual sibling convention.
questions.theory: Coded kinship relations translate symbols into directed family statements. The expression is a chain of pairwise statements, not arithmetic with ordinary precedence. “P is brother of Q” establishes that P is male and P,Q are siblings; “P is sister of Q” establishes P is female; “P is father of Q” establishes a parent-child direction and P’s sex. A niece is a female child of one’s sibling, so both generation and sex must be proved. The method is to translate every adjacent pair and draw or mentally track the family tree. Do not infer the second person’s sex from the first person’s sibling title, and do not reverse a father relation. Standard aptitude questions assume ordinary shared parentage for stated siblings.

similar_questions.prompt: X is sister of Y; Y is father of Z; Z is sister of W. How is Z related to X?
similar_questions.solution: Z is female and daughter of Y, who is X’s sibling. Therefore Z is X’s niece.

similar_questions.prompt: A is brother of B and B is mother of C, who is male. How is C related to A?
similar_questions.solution: C is a male child of A’s sibling B, so C is A’s nephew.

The circles in the upper-left, upper-right and lower-left diamond portions have black halves respectively right, bottom and top. The lower-right quadrant is blank.

options.C: Falling diagonal; circle below-left with black left half

Follow the half-black circle through successive clockwise quarter-turns.
questions.solution: The missing lower-right quadrant needs a rising diagonal from the bottom midpoint of the whole square to the right midpoint. That excludes C. Circles are related by rotations about the whole figure’s center: the upper-left right-black circle rotates clockwise to the upper-right bottom-black circle, then to a lower-right left-black circle, then to the lower-left top-black circle. A rotation about a center sends all positions and orientations through the same angle; rotating a half-shaded circle changes which side is black even though its circular outline is unchanged. Here the square’s four quadrants form a cycle under clockwise ninety-degree rotations, and the diagonal segments must join into a closed diamond. The method is to analyze boundary geometry independently, then check symbol placement and shading orientation using the same symmetry. A candidate satisfying only one feature is insufficient. Common pitfalls include reflecting a symbol when the pattern calls for rotation, or keeping the black half fixed relative to the page instead of rotating it.

similar_questions.prompt: A top-black circle is rotated clockwise by 180 degrees. Which half is black?

questions.solution: ∇f=(2x−4y²,−8xy+3y²). At (1,0) this is (2,0), hence 2α=6/5 and α=3/5. At (1,1) the gradient is (−2,−5), so −2(3/5)−5β=14/5, giving β=−4/5. These components have unit norm, consistent with a direction vector. Thus 25(α−β)²=25(7/5)²=49.
questions.theory: For a differentiable scalar field f on Euclidean space, the directional derivative along a unit vector u is D_u f(a)=∇f(a)·u. Differentiability is the hypothesis ensuring that all directional derivatives arise from the same linear map. The gradient consists of the partial derivatives and points in the direction of maximal instantaneous increase. Several prescribed directional derivatives give linear equations for the components of a common direction. Solve those equations and check the unit-length condition when “direction” is conventionally normalized. A nonunit parametrization scales the derivative by its speed, so normalization must not be ignored. The method here is direct differentiation followed by a two-equation linear system, without estimating differences numerically.

similar_questions.prompt: For f=x²+y², find D_u f(1,2) for u=(3/5,4/5).

similar_questions.solution: Cauchy–Schwarz gives ∇f·u≤||∇f||=5. Equality is attained at u=(3/5,4/5).

questions.prompt: Let P₃₀(ℝ) be the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most 30. A linear transformation T:P₃₀(ℝ)→P₃₀(ℝ) satisfies T²=0. Find the maximum possible rank(T).
hints: T²=0 forces image(T) to lie inside kernel(T).
Use rank-nullity in the 31-dimensional polynomial space.
questions.solution: The basis 1,x,…,x³⁰ has 31 elements. T²=0 implies im T⊆ker T. If rank T=r, nullity is 31−r, so r≤31−r and r≤15. This is attainable: on a basis e₁,…,e₃₁ set T(e₁₆)=e₁,…,T(e₃₀)=e₁₅, and let all other basis vectors map to zero. Then T²=0 and rank T=15.
questions.theory: A square-zero linear operator satisfies T(Tv)=0 for every vector v, so every image vector lies in the kernel. Rank-nullity states that rank(T)+nullity(T)=dim V for an operator on a finite-dimensional space. The inclusion im T⊆ker T therefore yields rank(T)≤dim V/2. A maximum-rank construction pairs basis vectors into length-two chains v↦w↦0; an unpaired basis vector maps to zero. Equivalently, its nilpotent Jordan blocks have size at most two. Remember that the space of polynomials of degree at most n has dimension n+1, because the constant polynomial belongs to the basis. A bound alone does not prove a maximum: an example attaining it is required.

similar_questions.prompt: Find maximum rank of a square-zero operator on ℝ⁸.
similar_questions.solution: Image lies in kernel, so r≤8−r and r≤4. Mapping e₅,…,e₈ to e₁,…,e₄ and the latter to zero attains rank 4.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a square-zero operator on a 5-dimensional space have rank 3?
similar_questions.solution: Rank 3 would give kernel dimension 2, contradicting containment of a 3-dimensional image in the kernel. Maximum rank is 2.

questions.prompt: Let A=[[4,2,−1],[1,5,3],[2,2,5]]. In the Gauss–Seidel scheme for Ax=b, x⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾=Gx⁽ᵏ⁾+c. Find trace(G).

Successively substitute the newly updated first and second coordinates into later updates.
questions.solution: For the homogeneous error update, x₁′=−x₂/2+x₃/4. Next x₂′=−x₁′/5−3x₃/5=x₂/10−13x₃/20. Finally x₃′=−2x₁′/5−2x₂′/5=4x₂/25+4x₃/25. Thus G has diagonal entries 0,1/10,4/25, and trace=1/10+4/25=13/50. The affine vector involving b does not affect G.
questions.theory: Gauss–Seidel iteration solves the equations sequentially, using newly updated coordinates as soon as they are available. If A=D+L+U with diagonal D, strictly lower L and strictly upper U, the iteration matrix is G=−(D+L)⁻¹U, assuming the diagonal entries are nonzero. The constant vector is (D+L)⁻¹b. Jacobi iteration instead uses only old coordinates and has matrix −D⁻¹(L+U), so their traces generally differ. Convergence for every initial vector occurs when the spectral radius ρ(G)<1; trace by itself is not a convergence criterion. To compute G economically, update homogeneous errors coordinate by coordinate and read off old-coordinate coefficients. Be careful to distinguish new from old variables.

similar_questions.prompt: Find Gauss–Seidel G for A=[[2,1],[1,2]].
similar_questions.solution: Errors update as x₁′=−x₂/2 and x₂′=−x₁′/2=x₂/4. Thus G=[[0,−1/2],[0,1/4]], with trace 1/4.

similar_questions.prompt: For diagonal A=diag(2,3), what is the Gauss–Seidel iteration matrix?
similar_questions.solution: There are no off-diagonal terms, so each update directly sets x₁=b₁/2,x₂=b₂/3. Error is eliminated in one step and G=0.

questions.prompt: On M₃(ℝ), define T(A)=Aᵀ. Consider S1: T is diagonalizable; S2: trace(T)=6. Which is true?
hints: Split matrices into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts.
The transpose acts as +1 and −1 on those two subspaces.
questions.solution: Every A has the unique decomposition A=(A+Aᵀ)/2+(A−Aᵀ)/2. The symmetric subspace has dimension 3(4)/2=6 and eigenvalue +1; the skew-symmetric subspace has dimension 3(2)/2=3 and eigenvalue −1. Their direct sum is all nine-dimensional M₃(ℝ), so T is diagonalizable. Its trace as a linear operator is 6−3=3, not 6. Thus only S1 is true.
questions.theory: A linear operator is diagonalizable if its domain has a basis of eigenvectors. Over a field of characteristic different from two, every matrix splits uniquely into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts. Transposition fixes the former and negates the latter, giving eigenspaces for eigenvalues +1 and −1. For n×n matrices their dimensions are n(n+1)/2 and n(n−1)/2, summing to n². The trace of the transpose operator is therefore n, not the dimension of its fixed space. Another proof uses T²=I: the minimal polynomial divides (t−1)(t+1), which has distinct roots over ℝ. A pitfall is confusing the operator trace with the trace of a particular input matrix or with a single eigenvalue multiplicity.

similar_questions.prompt: Find eigenvalue multiplicities and trace of transpose on M₂(ℝ).
similar_questions.solution: Symmetric matrices form a 3-dimensional +1 eigenspace; skew-symmetric matrices form a 1-dimensional −1 eigenspace. Trace=3−1=2.

similar_questions.prompt: For T(A)=−Aᵀ on M₃(ℝ), find trace and diagonalizability.
similar_questions.solution: Symmetric matrices now have eigenvalue −1 with multiplicity 6; skew-symmetric matrices have +1 with multiplicity 3. The operator is diagonalizable and trace=−6+3=−3.

questions.prompt: Count integer solutions of x₁+x₂+x₃=17 with 0≤x₁≤7, 0≤x₂≤8, 0≤x₃≤12.
hints: Start with nonnegative solutions using stars and bars.
Subtract solutions violating each upper bound and add back overlaps.
questions.solution: Without upper bounds there are C(19,2)=171 solutions. Violations x₁≥8,x₂≥9,x₃≥13 give respectively C(11,2)=55,C(10,2)=45,C(6,2)=15 after shifting the violating coordinate. The joint first-second violation has residual sum 17−8−9=0, so contributes one solution. Other pair and triple violations are impossible. Inclusion–exclusion gives 171−55−45−15+1=57.
questions.theory: Stars and bars counts nonnegative integer solutions of x₁+⋯+x_k=N as C(N+k−1,k−1). Upper bounds require inclusion–exclusion: the event x_i≥u_i+1 can be counted by replacing x_i with y_i+u_i+1, leaving a smaller nonnegative sum. For intersections shift every offending coordinate; if the remaining total is negative there are no solutions. Inclusion–exclusion alternately subtracts single violations, adds pair overlaps, subtracts triple overlaps, and so on. The variables must be integers and the bounds inclusive. A common pitfall is shifting by u_i instead of u_i+1, thereby excluding valid boundary values. Another is forgetting overlaps after subtracting individual violation counts, which counts doubly invalid solutions incorrectly.

similar_questions.prompt: Count x+y=10 with 0≤x≤6 and 0≤y≤7.
similar_questions.solution: There are 11 unrestricted solutions. x≥7 contributes 4 and y≥8 contributes 3; their intersection is impossible. Count=11−4−3=4, corresponding to x=3,4,5,6.

similar_questions.prompt: Count x+y+z=4 with each variable at most 2.
similar_questions.solution: Unrestricted count=C(6,2)=15. Each violation ≥3 leaves sum 1, giving C(3,2)=3. Pair violations impossible. Count=15−3×3=6.

hints: Try the feasible ray with x₁=x₂=0 and increasing x₃.
Weak duality rules out any feasible dual point when the primal tends to −∞.
questions.solution: For x=(0,0,t), t≥5, both constraints hold and z=−4t→−∞. Thus the primal is feasible and unbounded below. If the dual had any feasible point, weak duality would give a finite lower bound on every primal objective, a contradiction. Hence the dual is infeasible. Directly, its variables satisfy y₁≥0,y₂≤0 and 2y₁−y₂≤−4 from the third column, impossible because the left side is nonnegative.
questions.theory: Linear-programming duality relates a primal minimization problem to a dual maximization problem. For nonnegative primal variables, dual constraints are Aᵀy≤c; a primal ≥ constraint yields a nonnegative dual multiplier, whereas a ≤ constraint yields a nonpositive multiplier. Weak duality states that every feasible dual objective is a lower bound for every feasible primal objective. Consequently, a feasible primal that is unbounded below forces dual infeasibility. The converse requires care: dual infeasibility alone does not distinguish primal infeasibility from primal unboundedness without more information. A convenient method is to find a feasible improving ray, then use weak duality or check the dual sign constraints directly. Be especially careful with mixed constraint directions.

similar_questions.prompt: Minimize −x subject to x≥1, x≥0. Determine the dual status.
similar_questions.solution: The primal is feasible and unbounded below. The dual is maximize y with y≥0 and y≤−1, hence infeasible.

questions.prompt: Let f:[0,1]→ℝ satisfy f(0)=0 and f(x)=(−1)ⁿ(1+n) for 1/(n+1)<x≤1/n, n∈ℕ. S1: ∫₀¹f(x)dx converges. S2: ∫₀¹|f(x)|dx diverges. Which is true?
hints: Multiply each step height by its interval length.
Check the remainder when the improper-integral cutoff falls inside an interval.
questions.solution: The nth interval length is 1/n−1/(n+1)=1/[n(n+1)]. Its signed integral is (−1)ⁿ/n. Thus the integral at endpoint cutoffs is the alternating harmonic series, which converges (to −log 2). For a cutoff within the nth interval, the omitted partial interval has absolute integral at most 1/n→0, so the full improper limit exists. For |f| the interval integrals are 1/n and their sum diverges. Both statements are true, interpreting the integrals as improper at 0; f is unbounded and is not a proper Riemann-integrable or Lebesgue-integrable function.
questions.theory: An improper integral at an endpoint is defined as a one-sided limit of integrals over compact subintervals away from that endpoint. It can converge conditionally, meaning the signed integral exists while the integral of the absolute value diverges. For a step function, interval integrals are height times width, so convergence can reduce to a series. Endpoint-cutoff series convergence alone should be supplemented by a bound on the partial final interval to establish convergence for arbitrary cutoffs. The alternating-series theorem applies when positive magnitudes decrease to zero; the harmonic series diverges. Lebesgue integrability of a real function requires absolute integrability and therefore differs from conditional improper convergence. A pitfall is calling an unbounded function properly Riemann integrable on the closed interval.

similar_questions.prompt: On (1/(n+1),1/n], let g=(−1)ⁿn(n+1)/n². Determine integrability near 0.
similar_questions.solution: Each signed interval integral is (−1)ⁿ/n² and each absolute integral is 1/n². Since Σ1/n² converges and the remainder is bounded by 1/n², the improper integral converges absolutely.

similar_questions.prompt: On the same intervals let h=n(n+1). Does its improper integral converge?
similar_questions.solution: Each interval contributes n(n+1)×1/[n(n+1)]=1. The total is Σ1, which diverges to +∞.

questions.theory: A second-order linear PDE in two variables has principal part Auₓₓ+2Buₓᵧ+Cuᵧᵧ. First-order terms and the zeroth-order term do not affect this classification. The coefficient of uₓᵧ is 2B, so forgetting the factor two gives an incorrect discriminant. When coefficients depend on position, type can vary across curves and regions. The method is to isolate principal coefficients, factor the zero-discriminant equation and examine the branch near the requested point. questions.prompt: Let P=[[1,−1,−1],[0,1,0],[0,1,2]], Q=[[1,1,0],[0,2,0],[0,0,1]], R=[[2,0,0],[0,1,−1],[1,0,1]]. Here ∼ denotes similarity and ≁ nonsimilarity. Which statement is true?

Compute ranks of P−I,Q−I,R−I.
questions.solution: All characteristic polynomials are (λ−1)²(λ−2). P−I=[[0,−1,−1],[0,0,0],[0,1,1]] and Q−I=[[0,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]] have rank 1, so their eigenvalue-1 eigenspaces have dimension 2. Each is diagonalizable and similar to diag(1,1,2), hence P∼Q. R−I=[[1,0,0],[0,0,−1],[1,0,0]] has rank 2, so its eigenvalue-1 eigenspace has dimension 1. It is not diagonalizable, and cannot be similar to Q. Thus A.
questions.theory: Similar matrices represent the same linear operator in different bases: B=S⁻¹AS with S invertible. Similarity preserves characteristic polynomial, minimal polynomial, eigenvalue multiplicities and dimensions of eigenspaces. Equal characteristic polynomials alone do not ensure similarity because Jordan block sizes can differ. A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when its eigenspaces span the full space; the geometric multiplicity of λ is nullity(A−λI). With one eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity two and another simple eigenvalue, the repeated eigenspace dimension decides whether a size-two Jordan block is present. The method is to compute eigenvalues, then use ranks of shifted matrices to distinguish the possible Jordan forms. Avoid concluding similarity solely from matching traces or determinants.

similar_questions.prompt: Are diag(1,1) and [[1,1],[0,1]] similar?
similar_questions.solution: Both have characteristic polynomial (λ−1)². The first has a 2-dimensional 1-eigenspace and the second a 1-dimensional one. They are not similar.

similar_questions.prompt: Are diag(2,3) and [[2,1],[0,3]] similar?

questions.prompt: X₁,…,Xₙ are sampled from f(x|θ)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1, θ>0. Which statement is FALSE?

options.A: ΣXᵢ/(n−ΣXᵢ) is the method-of-moments estimator of θ
options.B: −n/ΣlogₑXᵢ is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ
options.C: n/(n−ΣlogₑXᵢ) is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ/(1+θ)

hints: Compute Eθ[X] and maximize n log θ+(θ−1)Σlog Xᵢ.
Use invariance of maximum likelihood for the two transformed parameters.
questions.solution: Eθ[X]=θ/(θ+1). Equating this with X̄ gives θ_MM=X̄/(1−X̄)=ΣXᵢ/(n−ΣXᵢ), proving A. Let S=Σlog Xᵢ<0. The log likelihood has derivative n/θ+S and second derivative −n/θ²<0; θ̂=−n/S, proving B. Invariance gives θ̂/(1+θ̂)=n/(n−S), proving C. Similarly 2θ̂/(1+θ̂)=2n/(n−S), whereas D has n+S in the denominator. Thus D is false.
questions.theory: Method of moments estimates parameters by equating sample moments to their theoretical counterparts. For this one-parameter density on (0,1), direct integration gives Eθ[X]=θ/(θ+1), an invertible mean relation. Maximum likelihood chooses a parameter maximizing the product density, or equivalently the log likelihood. A negative second derivative and appropriate boundary behavior establish a unique global interior maximum. The invariance principle states that applying a function g to a maximum-likelihood estimate gives a maximum-likelihood estimate of g(θ), particularly straightforward for one-to-one transformations. Logarithms of observations in (0,1) are negative, so their sign is crucial. A common pitfall is simplifying a transformed estimate with the wrong denominator sign or treating a method-of-moments estimate as the likelihood estimate.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=2 observations e⁻¹ and e⁻³, find θ̂_ML.
similar_questions.solution: S=−1−3=−4, so θ̂=−2/(−4)=1/2. The log-likelihood second derivative is negative, confirming the maximum.

similar_questions.prompt: If X̄=3/4, find θ_MM and its transformed estimate θ/(1+θ).
similar_questions.solution: θ_MM=(3/4)/(1/4)=3. Applying the transform gives 3/4, exactly the original sample mean.

questions.prompt: A is a 2×2 positive definite matrix with trace(A−2I)=2 and det(A²−2I)=28. Find the determinant of the adjoint (adjugate) of A.

questions.solution: trace A−4=2, so s=trace A=6. Write d=det A>0. Since trace A²=s²−2d, det(A²−2I)=d²−2(s²−2d)+4=d²+4d−68=28. Hence d²+4d−96=0, with roots 8 and −12. Positive definiteness selects d=8. For a 2×2 matrix det(adj A)=det A, hence the answer is 8.
questions.theory: Trace and determinant of a two-dimensional matrix equal the sum and product of its eigenvalues, counted algebraically. The identity trace(A²)=(trace A)²−2det A follows from the characteristic polynomial or the eigenvalue relation λ₁²+λ₂²=(λ₁+λ₂)²−2λ₁λ₂. For a 2×2 matrix B, det(B−tI)=det B−t trace B+t². The classical adjugate satisfies A adj A=(det A)I and det(adj A)=(det A)^(n−1); in dimension two this is simply det A. Positive definiteness gives positive eigenvalues and positive determinant, allowing elimination of an extraneous algebraic root. Be careful that trace(A−2I)=trace A−2n, not trace A−2. Always verify the derived result by substituting it into the original hypotheses; this catches lost factors, extraneous roots and sign errors before comparing with the listed choices.

questions.prompt: A homogeneous Markov chain on {1,2,3,4} has transition matrix [[1,0,0,0],[1/2,1/4,1/4,0],[0,0,1/2,1/2],[0,0,1/4,3/4]]. Which statement is true?

State 2 can leave for a class from which no return to 2 is possible.
questions.solution: State 1 is absorbing, hence recurrent. States 3 and 4 communicate and form a finite closed class, so both are recurrent. From state 2 there is a 3/4 probability of leaving in one step for state 1 or 3, and no transition from those closed classes returns to 2. The probability of returning to 2 after time zero is only P₂₂=1/4<1. Therefore only state 2 is transient.
questions.theory: States of a Markov chain communicate if each is reachable from the other with positive probability. A communicating class is closed when no transition can leave it. In a finite state space every closed irreducible class consists of positive recurrent states; an absorbing singleton is a special case. A state is recurrent if the probability of ever returning after time zero is one, and transient if that probability is smaller than one. Self-loops alone do not imply recurrence: a state may loop for a while and then leave permanently. The method is to read the directed transition graph, identify closed classes and inspect whether remaining states can escape without return. Matrix rows, not columns, encode outgoing probabilities in the stated convention.

similar_questions.solution: State 2 is absorbing and recurrent. State 1 returns only if it self-loops initially; once it reaches 2 it never returns. Its return probability is 1/2, so it is transient.

similar_questions.prompt: For P=[[0,1],[1,0]], classify recurrence and period.

A one-to-one differentiable change of variable uses the absolute derivative of the inverse; the absolute value prevents a negative density under a decreasing transformation. Writing X=ΣⱼZⱼZⱼᵀ with independent standard normal Zⱼ gives trace(AX)=Σⱼ(Zⱼ1²+Zⱼ2²+aZⱼ1Zⱼ3). Its variance is n(4+a²), whereas χ²_(2n) has variance 4n; indeed the quadratic form can be negative. Thus D is not valid under the printed hypotheses, and no listed distribution is generally true. Conditional intended derivation: if A is additionally symmetric, orthogonal diagonalization makes A=diag(I_r,0), and trace(AX) is a sum of nr independent standard-normal squares, giving D. The missing symmetry is a genuine source issue.
questions.theory: The Wishart law W_p(n,I_p) is the distribution of a sum of n independent outer products ZZᵀ with Z a p-dimensional standard normal vector. The trace identity trace(AZZᵀ)=ZᵀAZ converts matrix functionals to quadratic forms. Such a form depends only on the symmetric part S=(A+Aᵀ)/2. A symmetric idempotent is an orthogonal projection, with r eigenvalues one and the rest zero; its quadratic form is χ²_r. Summing n independent copies gives χ²_nr. A nonsymmetric idempotent is not an orthogonal projection and its symmetric part need not be idempotent or positive semidefinite. The Gaussian formula Var(ZᵀSZ)=2trace(S²) exposes this difference. Never omit the symmetry hypothesis in applying the chi-square projection theorem.

Their total length is 1−1/π+(1/π)Σₖ≥1(1/(2k)−1/(2k+1)). The series equals 1−log 2 by the alternating harmonic series. Thus positive-side measure=1−log 2/π. Doubling gives 2−2log 2/π=(2/π)(π−log 2). Endpoints and zero are countable and do not affect measure.
questions.theory: Lebesgue outer measure equals Lebesgue measure for measurable sets, including countable unions of closed intervals. The function x sin(1/x), extended by zero, is continuous at zero because its absolute value is at most |x|, and is even. Its nonnegative set is therefore closed relative to the interval and measurable. To compute its measure, locate sign intervals of the sine function, invert their endpoints on the positive half-line, and add interval lengths; overlaps at endpoints have zero measure. Reciprocal substitution does not preserve lengths, so interval endpoints must be transformed explicitly. The alternating harmonic identity Σₙ≥1(−1)^(n−1)/n=log 2 evaluates the resulting series. A common pitfall is assuming equal sine half-periods correspond to equal x-interval lengths.

These properties also imply closure under finite intersections and set differences. When finitely many generators are given, their membership patterns divide Ω into disjoint nonempty atoms. Every set in the generated field is a union of atoms, and with k atoms there are exactly 2^k distinct unions. The smallest field containing the generators includes all such unions; counting how many are already present gives the minimum additions. Here the half-open interval endpoints matter when describing the remaining atom. Do not count only complements of the original sets and forget unions of newly created sets.

Finding its order does not require constructing it or counting how many such subgroups exist. The method is to count independent column choices, factor the resulting integer and extract the relevant valuation. Do not count all q^(n²) matrices, since singular matrices must be excluded.

questions.theory: A differential initial-value problem can be converted into a Volterra integral equation by taking its highest derivative as the unknown. Repeated integration reconstructs lower derivatives using initial values; for a second derivative u, y(x)=y(0)+xy′(0)+∫₀ˣ(x−t)u(t)dt. For such p, the V conditions are 4c₂+12c₃+32c₄=0 and −8c₂−26c₃−80c₄=0. These rows are independent, so dim(V∩W)=3−2=1. Therefore dim(V+W)=3+3−1=5.
questions.theory: Linear evaluation and derivative conditions define kernels of linear maps on polynomial spaces. Their codimension equals the rank of the condition matrix, not automatically the number of printed equations, so independence must be checked. The polynomial space P_n has dimension n+1. For subspaces V,W, the dimension formula is dim(V+W)=dim V+dim W−dim(V∩W). A convenient basis can simplify constraints: centering powers at the derivative evaluation point exposes odd/even coefficients, while vanishing value and derivative at zero means divisibility by x². The method is to compute individual dimensions and then restrict one subspace’s coefficients to the other’s constraints. A pitfall is forgetting the overlap and obtaining a sum dimension larger than the ambient space.

questions.prompt: For one observation X, test H₀:f(x)=6x⁵, 0<x<1, against H₁:f(x)=10x⁹. What is the power of the most powerful test of size 0.1?

Choose an upper-tail cutoff from the null CDF x⁶, then evaluate the alternative tail x¹⁰.
questions.solution: The likelihood ratio is (10x⁹)/(6x⁵)=(5/3)x⁴, increasing in x. By Neyman–Pearson reject for x>c. Null size is 1−c⁶=0.1, giving c⁶=0.9. Under H₁ the power is 1−c¹⁰=1−(0.9)^(10/6)=1−(9/10)^(5/3). The test is most powerful for this simple alternative, and its monotone-likelihood-ratio form also fits a larger increasing-exponent family.
questions.theory: The Neyman–Pearson lemma characterizes a most powerful level-α test of a simple null against a simple alternative by rejecting where the likelihood ratio f₁/f₀ exceeds a cutoff. If the ratio is strictly increasing in the observation, the rejection region is an upper tail; if decreasing it is a lower tail. The cutoff is selected using the null distribution so its rejection probability equals the prescribed size. Power is the rejection probability under the alternative distribution, which must be evaluated separately. For densities θx^(θ−1) on (0,1), the CDF is x^θ. No randomization is needed for a continuous distribution at a single cutoff. A common pitfall is using the alternative law to set the size threshold.

similar_questions.solution: Likelihood ratio=2x² is increasing, so reject x>c. Null gives 1−c²=1/4, hence c²=3/4. Power=1−c⁴=1−9/16=7/16.

questions.solution: A matches III: generalized coordinates need not correspond to perpendicular Cartesian directions. D matches II: conservative forces are derived from potential energy. C matches IV: a sphere rolling without slipping on a plane has nonholonomic constraints. The remaining intended rheonomic example, a vibrator with explicitly time-dependent imposed motion, matches B to I. Therefore A-III,B-I,C-IV,D-II, option C. “Vibrators” is a shorthand here for driven time-dependent constraints, since free vibration alone does not imply rheonomic constraints.
questions.theory: Generalized coordinates are independent parameters describing a mechanical configuration, chosen to suit its constraints; angles and curvilinear coordinates need not correspond to mutually perpendicular directions. Holonomic constraints can be written as equations of coordinates and time, while nonholonomic constraints generally involve velocities and cannot be integrated into such configuration equations. A rheonomic constraint depends explicitly on time; a scleronomic one does not. A conservative force admits a scalar potential, with generalized forces obtained from its negative derivatives, and its work depends only on endpoints under the usual conditions. Rolling without slipping for a sphere provides nonintegrable velocity constraints. The method in a matching question is to anchor precise definitions first and then interpret shorthand examples consistently. Do not equate any oscillating motion with an explicitly time-dependent constraint.
